speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I understand you have knee pain after increasing your physical activity; to help me narrow down the cause, could you describe exactly where the pain is located and what specific movements make it worse?

speaker: Patient
text: 23-year-old female. The patient presents with knee pain that started yesterday and has been steadily worsening. She cites recent participation in volleyball involving repetitive pivoting and twisting movements as a possible cause. She was advised at her last physical exam that weight loss could be beneficial for her health.

speaker: Doctor
text: Based on the history of repetitive pivoting and twisting during volleyball, could you tell me if you heard a "pop" at the time of injury, and have you noticed any swelling or an inability to fully straighten your knee?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Knee pain, specifically over the medial aspect of the tibia just inferior to the patella. I also have Recent weight loss attempt, Increased physical activity.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the details. The pain located on the medial aspect of the tibia just inferior to the patella is a key finding; have you noticed any tenderness specifically at the pes anserine bursa or along the medial tibial crest when I touch it? Additionally, does the pain worsen significantly with prolonged walking or going up/down stairs?

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Pes Anserine Bursitis. The clinical presentation of medial tibial pain inferior to the patella, exacerbated by stair climbing and confirmed by tenderness at the pes anserine location, combined with recent increased activity, is diagnostic. The ultrasound ruled out significant fluid collections, supporting an inflammatory rather than infectious or septic etiology.
